reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone
clinicalPearls: The most common benign bone tumour, typically arising from the metaphysis of long bones about the knee and the proximal humerus and pointing away from the adjacent joint.
The pathognomonic feature is continuity of both the cortex and the medullary cavity of the lesion with those of the host bone, best demonstrated on CT or MRI.
It may be pedunculated (stalked) or sessile (broad-based) and grows only until skeletal maturity; continued growth thereafter is a warning sign.
Complications include mechanical impingement, formation of an overlying bursa, fracture of a pedunculated stalk, and compression of adjacent nerves or vessels, including popliteal pseudoaneurysm.
The cartilage cap is thin in adults; a cap thicker than roughly 1.5 to 2 cm on MRI raises concern for transformation to secondary peripheral chondrosarcoma.

Hereditary multiple exostoses is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by EXT1 or EXT2 mutations, producing multiple lesions, short stature and forearm deformity with a higher risk of malignant transformation.
Malignant transformation occurs in roughly 1 per cent of solitary lesions but is appreciably more frequent in hereditary multiple exostoses.
Symptomatic lesions or those suspected of transformation are excised, taking the cartilage cap and overlying perichondrium to minimise recurrence.
reference.pathophysiology: Osteochondroma is a cartilage-capped bony projection arising on the external surface of a bone, regarded as a developmental lesion in which a fragment of physeal cartilage herniates through a defect in the perichondrial ring of Ranvier, separates from the growth plate and continues to grow by endochondral ossification. Because it originates from the physis, the lesion enlarges only during skeletal growth and characteristically maintains corticomedullary continuity with the parent bone. Biallelic inactivation of the tumour suppressor genes EXT1 or EXT2, which encode glycosyltransferases required for heparan sulfate biosynthesis, disrupts the diffusion gradients of signalling molecules that regulate chondrocyte proliferation; germline EXT mutations underlie hereditary multiple exostoses, while sporadic solitary lesions harbour somatic EXT alterations.
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs to demonstrate the surface lesion and its relationship to the joint
CT to confirm corticomedullary continuity with the host bone
MRI to measure cartilage cap thickness and detect any soft-tissue mass
Clinical assessment and family history to identify hereditary multiple exostoses
Vascular imaging or angiography when a vascular complication such as pseudoaneurysm is suspected
Comparison with prior imaging to document growth after skeletal maturity
redFlags: Pain or documented growth after skeletal maturity
Cartilage cap thicker than about 2 cm on MRI
A new or enlarging soft-tissue mass overlying the lesion
Irregular, lucent or destructive areas developing within a previously stable lesion
Sudden neurovascular symptoms suggesting compression or pseudoaneurysm
reference.prognosis: Solitary osteochondroma has an excellent prognosis, with recurrence occurring mainly after incomplete excision of the cartilage cap. Malignant transformation is uncommon overall but is an important long-term consideration, particularly in hereditary multiple exostoses.
pitfalls: Mistaking a thick cartilage cap for a benign feature and missing early chondrosarcomatous transformation
Overlooking the diagnosis of hereditary multiple exostoses and its familial and malignancy implications
Incomplete excision leaving perichondrium and cap, leading to recurrence
Failing to recognise vascular injury such as popliteal artery pseudoaneurysm from a stalked lesion
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone (current edition)
